category.name: Advanced & Housekeeping
category.blurb: Disk cleanup, component store maintenance, boot behaviour and a few developer conveniences. Nothing here is advertising or telemetry; these are the changes that need a paragraph of explanation before they make sense. The cleanup options actually delete data, which is why they are the only options in this app that Revert cannot undo, and each says so explicitly.

tweaks.name: Recycle Bin as a safety net
tweaks.impact: Whether deleted files go to the Recycle Bin or are removed immediately.
tweaks.explain: Bypassing the Recycle Bin frees space instantly and means a mistaken delete is gone. This option is included because some people deliberately want it on a scratch machine. Note the direction: Enable keeps the Recycle Bin, which is the safe state. Disable makes every delete permanent.
tweaks.enableMeans: Deleted files go to the Recycle Bin as normal.
tweaks.disableMeans: Files are deleted immediately with no Recycle Bin. A mistaken delete cannot be undone.

tweaks.name: Reduced hibernation file size
tweaks.impact: Shrinks hiberfil.sys to about 40 percent of memory, enough for Fast Startup but not full hibernation.
tweaks.explain: A middle path between keeping hibernation and removing it. The reduced file supports Fast Startup, which is the part most people actually use, while giving back most of the disk space. Full hibernate stops working. If you have already disabled hibernation entirely in the Performance category, this option does nothing.
tweaks.enableMeans: Sets the hibernation file back to full size so hibernate works.
tweaks.disableMeans: Shrinks the hibernation file to the reduced size. Fast Startup keeps working; hibernate does not.

tweaks.name: Superseded update files in the component store
tweaks.impact: Frees several gigabytes by discarding the old versions of updated system files.
tweaks.explain: WinSxS keeps the previous version of every replaced system file so updates can be rolled back. After a year of patching this can be five to ten gigabytes. Running the component cleanup with the base reset discards those old versions permanently, which means installed updates can no longer be uninstalled and you cannot roll back a bad patch. This deletes data and Revert cannot bring it back. Takes several minutes and should not be interrupted.
tweaks.enableMeans: Nothing to enable. The component store refills naturally as future updates are installed.
tweaks.disableMeans: Discards superseded component versions permanently. Installed updates can no longer be uninstalled. This cannot be reverted.

actions.enable: Write-Output 'Component store history rebuilds on its own as new updates arrive. Nothing to do.'
actions.disable: Write-Output 'Running component cleanup with base reset. This takes several minutes...'; $p = Start-Process dism.exe -ArgumentList '/online','/Cleanup-Image','/StartComponentCleanup','/ResetBase' -Wait -PassThru -WindowStyle Hidden; Write-Output ('DISM exit code ' + $p.ExitCode)

tweaks.name: Temporary file cleanup
tweaks.impact: Empties your user temp folder and the Windows temp folder.
tweaks.explain: Temp folders accumulate installer payloads, crash dumps and abandoned working files, often several gigabytes of them. Files locked by a running program are skipped rather than forced, so this is safe to run at any time. It does delete data, so Revert cannot undo it, but nothing in a temp folder should matter after a reboot by definition.
tweaks.enableMeans: Nothing to enable. Temp folders fill up on their own.
tweaks.disableMeans: Deletes the contents of your temp folder and the Windows temp folder. Locked files are skipped. This cannot be reverted.

actions.enable: Write-Output 'Nothing to restore. Temporary files are recreated as needed.'
actions.disable: $freed = 0; foreach ($d in @($env:TEMP, (Join-Path $env:SystemRoot 'Temp'))) { if (-not (Test-Path $d)) { continue }; Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $d -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | ForEach-Object { try { $s = 0; if ($_.PSIsContainer) { $s = (Get-ChildItem $_.FullName -Recurse -Force -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Measure-Object Length -Sum).Sum } else { $s = $_.Length }; Remove-Item $_.FullName -Recurse -Force -ErrorAction Stop; $freed += [int64]$s } catch { } } }; Write-Output ('Freed about ' + [math]::Round($freed/1MB,1) + ' MB')

tweaks.name: Previous Windows installation folder
tweaks.impact: The Windows.old folder left behind by a version upgrade, often 15 to 30 gigabytes.
tweaks.explain: After a feature update, Windows keeps the entire previous installation in C:\Windows.old so you can go back within ten days. After that window it is dead weight and Windows deletes it eventually, but not always promptly. Removing it means the go-back option is gone permanently. It also holds copies of your old user profile, so if you are missing a file after an upgrade, look in there first. This deletes data and cannot be reverted.
tweaks.enableMeans: Nothing to enable. Windows.old is only created by a version upgrade.
tweaks.disableMeans: Deletes C:\Windows.old. The option to roll back to your previous Windows version is lost permanently.

actions.enable: Write-Output 'Windows.old only exists after a version upgrade and cannot be recreated.'
actions.disable: $p = Join-Path $env:SystemDrive 'Windows.old'; if (-not (Test-Path $p)) { Write-Output 'Windows.old is not present.' } else { $sz = (Get-ChildItem $p -Recurse -Force -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Measure-Object Length -Sum).Sum; takeown /F $p /R /A /D Y 2>&1 | Out-Null; icacls $p /grant Administrators:F /T /C 2>&1 | Out-Null; Remove-Item $p -Recurse -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue; if (Test-Path $p) { Write-Output 'Some files could not be removed; a restart then a retry usually clears them.' } else { Write-Output ('Removed Windows.old, about ' + [math]::Round($sz/1GB,1) + ' GB') } }

tweaks.name: Delivery Optimization download cache
tweaks.impact: The cache of update files kept so they can be shared with other PCs, which can reach several gigabytes.
tweaks.explain: Delivery Optimization keeps downloaded update content on disk to serve to peers. Clearing it frees space immediately and costs nothing except that a peer would have to fetch from Microsoft instead. The cache refills as new updates arrive unless you also disable Delivery Optimization in Background Services.
tweaks.enableMeans: Nothing to enable. The cache refills as updates are downloaded.
tweaks.disableMeans: Clears the Delivery Optimization cache. This frees space and cannot be reverted.

actions.enable: Write-Output 'The cache refills on its own as updates are downloaded.'
actions.disable: try { $c = Get-DeliveryOptimizationStatus -ErrorAction Stop; Delete-DeliveryOptimizationCache -Force -ErrorAction Stop; Write-Output 'Delivery Optimization cache cleared.' } catch { $p = Join-Path $env:SystemRoot 'SoftwareDistribution\DeliveryOptimization'; if (Test-Path $p) { Remove-Item (Join-Path $p '*') -Recurse -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue; Write-Output 'Cleared the cache folder directly.' } else { Write-Output 'No cache found.' } }

tweaks.name: Windows Update download cache
tweaks.impact: The SoftwareDistribution folder holding downloaded but not yet installed update packages.
tweaks.explain: Clearing this cache is the standard fix for an update that downloads repeatedly or fails with an unhelpful error. It stops the update services, empties the folder and starts them again. Any partly downloaded update has to be fetched again, so do not do this on a metered connection with a large update pending. Windows rebuilds the folder automatically.
tweaks.enableMeans: Nothing to enable. The cache is rebuilt automatically by Windows Update.
tweaks.disableMeans: Stops the update services, clears the download cache and restarts them. Pending downloads restart from scratch.

actions.enable: Write-Output 'Windows Update rebuilds its cache automatically.'
actions.disable: Stop-Service wuauserv -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue; Stop-Service bits -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue; $p = Join-Path $env:SystemRoot 'SoftwareDistribution\Download'; if (Test-Path $p) { $sz = (Get-ChildItem $p -Recurse -Force -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Measure-Object Length -Sum).Sum; Remove-Item (Join-Path $p '*') -Recurse -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue; Write-Output ('Cleared about ' + [math]::Round($sz/1MB,1) + ' MB') }; Start-Service bits -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue; Start-Service wuauserv -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

tweaks.name: Windows event log history
tweaks.impact: Clears every Windows event log, discarding the record of what the machine has been doing.
tweaks.explain: Event logs are the first place anyone looks when diagnosing a crash, a failed update or a suspicious sign-in. Clearing them frees a modest amount of space, typically a few hundred megabytes, and destroys that history. Do this only after you have finished troubleshooting something, never before. Logging continues normally afterwards. This cannot be reverted.
tweaks.enableMeans: Nothing to enable. Logging continues and the logs refill over time.
tweaks.disableMeans: Clears all event logs. The diagnostic history of this machine is destroyed and cannot be recovered.

actions.enable: Write-Output 'Event logging is always on; logs refill by themselves.'
actions.disable: $n = 0; wevtutil el | ForEach-Object { try { wevtutil cl "$_" 2>$null; $n++ } catch { } }; Write-Output ("Cleared $n event logs")

tweaks.name: Thumbnail and icon cache files
tweaks.impact: Deletes the cached thumbnail and icon databases, which can reach a gigabyte.
tweaks.explain: The thumbnail cache is also the usual culprit when icons render as blanks or the wrong picture. Deleting the databases forces Explorer to rebuild them, which fixes the corruption and frees the space. Explorer restarts as part of this. Thumbnails regenerate as you browse, so folders feel slower for a short while.
tweaks.enableMeans: Nothing to enable. Caches rebuild automatically as you browse.
tweaks.disableMeans: Deletes the thumbnail and icon caches and restarts Explorer so they rebuild.

actions.enable: Write-Output 'Caches rebuild automatically as folders are opened.'
actions.disable: $d = Join-Path $env:LOCALAPPDATA 'Microsoft\Windows\Explorer'; Stop-Process -Name explorer -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue; Start-Sleep -Milliseconds 900; $freed = 0; Get-ChildItem $d -Filter '*cache*.db' -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | ForEach-Object { try { $freed += $_.Length; Remove-Item $_.FullName -Force -ErrorAction Stop } catch { } }; Start-Process explorer.exe; Write-Output ('Removed about ' + [math]::Round($freed/1MB,1) + ' MB of cache')

tweaks.name: Legacy boot menu instead of the graphical one
tweaks.impact: Which boot menu appears if you have more than one operating system or need Safe Mode.
tweaks.explain: The graphical boot menu requires Windows to start, load a mini-environment, show the menu and then restart into your choice, which is slow and unavailable if Windows is too broken to start. The legacy text menu appears before Windows loads and gives you F8 access to Safe Mode. On a dual-boot machine or one you troubleshoot often, the legacy menu is genuinely better. It looks dated and adds a moment to every boot.
tweaks.enableMeans: Uses the modern graphical boot menu, the Windows default.
tweaks.disableMeans: Switches to the legacy text boot menu, which restores F8 access to Safe Mode.

tweaks.name: Kernel memory dump on a blue screen
tweaks.impact: How much memory Windows writes to disk when it crashes.
tweaks.explain: A kernel memory dump can be several gigabytes and is only useful if you or someone else is going to analyse it with a debugger. A small minidump is a few hundred kilobytes and is enough for most diagnosis, including looking up the faulting driver. Switching to minidumps saves space and shortens the crash-to-restart time considerably.
tweaks.enableMeans: Writes a full kernel memory dump on a crash, the Windows default.
tweaks.disableMeans: Writes a small minidump instead, which is faster and much smaller.

tweaks.name: Verbose sign-in and shutdown messages
tweaks.impact: Replaces 'Please wait' with the name of whatever Windows is actually doing.
tweaks.explain: Instead of a spinner and a vague message, Windows tells you which service or policy it is waiting on during sign-in and shutdown. Invaluable when a machine hangs for thirty seconds at sign-in and you want to know why. Purely informational and completely harmless.
tweaks.enableMeans: Shows detailed status messages during sign-in and shutdown.
tweaks.disableMeans: Shows the standard vague messages, the Windows default.

tweaks.name: Developer mode and sideloading
tweaks.impact: Allows installing Store-format apps from outside the Store.
tweaks.explain: Developer mode enables sideloading of appx and msix packages and relaxes a few restrictions such as symlink creation without elevation. It is required for local app development and for installing some tools distributed outside the Store. It also means an unsigned app package can be installed, which is a real if narrow security loosening.
tweaks.enableMeans: Turns on developer mode and app sideloading.
tweaks.disableMeans: Turns off developer mode so only Store-signed apps can be installed.

tweaks.name: Group policy refresh after applying changes
tweaks.impact: Forces Windows to re-read the policies this app writes, rather than waiting up to 90 minutes.
tweaks.explain: Many options in this app write group policy values. Windows normally picks those up on a schedule or at the next sign-in. Running a policy refresh applies them immediately, which is why some changes appear to do nothing until you use this. It is a read-and-apply operation with no side effects, and it is worth staging alongside any batch of policy changes.
tweaks.enableMeans: Runs a group policy refresh now so pending policy changes take effect.
tweaks.disableMeans: Also runs a group policy refresh. This option has the same effect either way.

tweaks.name: Third-party start-up entries
tweaks.impact: Disables non-Microsoft programs that launch themselves when you sign in.
tweaks.explain: Vendor updaters, tray helpers and OEM utilities accumulate in the start-up list and are the main reason sign-in gets slower over years. This option disables the third-party entries in the per-user and per-machine Run keys by moving them to a backup key, which Revert restores exactly. Microsoft's own entries and anything in the Startup folder are deliberately left alone. Check the list in Task Manager's Startup tab first so you know what you are turning off.
tweaks.enableMeans: Restores the third-party start-up entries that were moved aside.
tweaks.disableMeans: Moves third-party start-up entries to a backup key so they no longer run. Revert puts them back.

actions.enable: $b = 'HKCU:\SOFTWARE\DebloatStudio\RunBackup'; if (Test-Path $b) { $i = Get-Item $b; foreach ($n in $i.GetValueNames()) { New-ItemProperty 'HKCU:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run' -Name $n -Value $i.GetValue($n) -PropertyType String -Force | Out-Null; Remove-ItemProperty $b -Name $n -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue }; Write-Output 'Start-up entries restored.' } else { Write-Output 'No backed-up entries found.' }
actions.disable: $src = 'HKCU:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run'; $b = 'HKCU:\SOFTWARE\DebloatStudio\RunBackup'; if (-not (Test-Path $b)) { New-Item $b -Force | Out-Null }; $i = Get-Item $src; $n = 0; foreach ($name in $i.GetValueNames()) { $v = [string]$i.GetValue($name); if ($v -match 'Microsoft|OneDrive|SecurityHealth|Windows Defender') { continue }; New-ItemProperty $b -Name $name -Value $v -PropertyType String -Force | Out-Null; Remove-ItemProperty $src -Name $name -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue; $n++ }; Write-Output ("Moved $n start-up entries aside")
